title.analysis: Authentic title "POV: You Stopped Following Normal Money Advice" uses the channel's POV second-person frame and a contrarian promise. The script compares two composite 32-year-olds (Nina, conventional; Ian, unconventional) across savings rate, car, house, advisor and credit cards. TYPICAL (1.00x) against peers that include two STRONG titles. Association only; no CTR or experiment evidence.

script.opening_words: It's a Tuesday night. You open your banking app. Not because you need to, just out of the quiet compulsion that develops when money is a low-grade anxiety that never fully goes away. Decent salary, 401k going in, credit card paid off every month. You're doing everything right. And the number on the screen looks almost exactly like it did 3 months ago. Not dramatically worse, just hovering. Your financial life is a lake that gets filled from one end
script.ending_words: payment, the stretched mortgage, the 4% savings rate, and the actively managed fund portfolio, that's the gamble. It's just a gamble that looks too normal to feel dangerous. Nina isn't reckless, she's just following a script written by people who get paid when she does. Ian isn't depriving himself. He's just the one whose Tuesday nights are quiet. The only question that matters now is which Tuesday night you want.
script.analysis: Full 18741 canonical characters read. A contrarian comparison: Tuesday-night banking-app hook, coworker retiring at 51, Nina vs Ian setup with 30-year outcomes, then line-by-line: 10% savings rate, savings rate vs years to FI, car payments and negative equity, $700/month invested, rent vs buy and Shiller housing returns, hidden home costs, 1% advisor fee and SPIVA, credit-card rewards and pain of paying, Ian's automated year, social-norm psychology and Dutch lottery neighbours, the playbook as a business model, a repeated outcome close and the median 401(k). Verified: median household income, CE spending, SPIVA 20-year (~95%), Vanguard $95,642 median, rent-vs-buy figures (but from March 2025). Reproduces: advisor fee $934K, $1.58M (at an unstated 10%), maintenance. Problems: Nina/Ian ages and horizons inconsistent (30 years vs "at 55" vs stopping at 51); $3.16M not reproducible from 35% of $60K at 8%; "$72,000 after tax" contradicts "around $60,000"; 20% day-one depreciation; MIT 12-18%; "physical pain" neuroscience. The stored ending is complete.

claim_audit.claim: In 30 years Nina has ~$952,000 net worth, a 401(k) yielding ~$38,000 vs $75,000 expenses, working to 66; Ian has ~$3,163,000 yielding $126,500, stopping at 51; a $2.2M gap.

claim_audit.assessment: K02: 3,163,000 - 952,000 = 2,211,000 and 126,500/3,163,000 = 4.0% (reproduce). The model inputs are not disclosed. Internal inconsistency: "30 years from now" at age 32 is 62, yet the close says "At 55" for both, and Ian stops at 51 while compounding 30 years. At 35% of $60,000 ($21,000/yr) at 8% for 30 years the result is $2.38M; $3.16M needs higher returns or rising contributions. Illustrative composite.

claim_audit.assessment: CENSUSINC2: 2024 median household income $83,730 (verified). BLSCE2: average annual expenditures $77,158 (2023) / $78,535 (2024).
